body:
Why disaster preparedness begins with the community

A disaster may affect an entire district, but its immediate consequences are experienced by people in particular villages, neighbourhoods, schools and workplaces. Residents often notice danger first, know which routes remain usable and can identify people who need assistance. This makes the community an essential participant in disaster preparedness and response.

Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction (CBDRR) is an approach in which local people actively participate in identifying disaster risks, assessing vulnerabilities and capacities, planning preventive measures, implementing preparedness activities and reviewing their effectiveness.

CBDRR is broader than asking residents to help after a disaster. Its purpose is to reduce risk before an emergency occurs while strengthening the community's ability to respond and recover. Government agencies provide authority, technical guidance and resources; community members contribute local knowledge, participation and sustained action.

Understanding the basic relationship between risk and preparedness

A hazard is a potentially harmful event or process, such as a flood, cyclone or earthquake. Exposure refers to people and assets located where a hazard may occur. Vulnerability refers to conditions that increase susceptibility to harm. Capacity includes the knowledge, resources, skills and arrangements that help people anticipate and manage danger.

For example, 2 households may live in the same flood-prone street. Both are exposed to flooding, but a household with limited mobility and no transport may face greater difficulty during evacuation. A nearby accessible shelter, advance warning and an agreed assistance arrangement can reduce that difficulty. Thus, similar exposure does not necessarily mean identical vulnerability.

Local knowledge as a preparedness resource

Local residents may know which roads become waterlogged, where drinking-water sources are located, which settlements are isolated during heavy rain and which buildings have previously been used for shelter. Farmers, fishers, transport workers, teachers and health workers may possess different parts of this knowledge.

Such information becomes more useful when it is collected systematically and checked against available hazard information, official warnings and assessments by competent authorities. Traditional observations can supplement preparedness, but they should not replace verified warnings or technical advice.

Participation, partnership and ownership

Participation means that people can express their experiences and influence decisions. Partnership means that community groups and institutions work together. Ownership means that local people understand the plan, accept responsibility for agreed tasks and continue maintaining it rather than treating it as an outside project.

Participation must extend beyond the most influential residents. Women, persons with disabilities, older people, people living in informal settlements, migrants and other groups may identify difficulties that a general village meeting overlooks. A plan prepared without their views may appear complete but remain unusable for some households.

Local self-government provides a suitable democratic setting for this work. In rural areas, the Gram Sabha enables residents to discuss local concerns, while the Gram Panchayat undertakes local functions and implements programmes within its powers. The Gram Sabha consists of persons registered in the electoral rolls of the village or villages within the Gram Panchayat area; the Gram Panchayat is the elected local body. They should not be treated as identical institutions.

The process of community-based risk reduction

The October 2024 national CBDRR guidelines describe an interconnected process in which communities organise, involve stakeholders, assess risk, implement activities and evaluate results. The process is repeated because hazards, settlement patterns, infrastructure and household needs can change.

Consider a coastal village in Gujarat. Residents may identify low-lying houses, agree on a safe gathering place, arrange assistance for people with limited mobility and practise reaching a designated shelter. After a drill, they may discover that a particular route is unsuitable during heavy rain. Revising the route is part of preparedness, not evidence that the original planning exercise was pointless.

Community ownership does not transfer the legal responsibility for disaster management from public authorities to residents. Local initiatives should be connected to official disaster plans, warnings, resources and response arrangements.

Prelims focus

  • CBDRR involves communities in risk identification, assessment, planning, implementation and evaluation.
  • Hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity are related but distinct concepts.
  • Local knowledge should complement verified hazard information and official warnings.
  • The October 2024 NDMA CBDRR guidelines describe 5 connected processes.
  • The Gram Sabha provides a forum for participation and accountability; the Gram Panchayat is the elected local body.
  • Trap: Community participation does not mean that government agencies cease to be responsible for disaster management.

[National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction, October 2024, executive summary, Chapter 2 and Sections 4.1–4.2; National Council of Educational Research and Training, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 8, Local Governments, printed pp. 177–180; National Council of Educational Research and Training, Social and Political Life–I, Class 6, Chapter 5, Panchayati Raj, printed pp. 43–48. Official guidelines consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Community-Based Disaster Preparedness: Meaning, Local Knowledge and Participation

body:
Why a community risk assessment must identify more than hazards

A hazard map shows where a potentially harmful event may occur. A useful community risk assessment goes further: it identifies who and what may be exposed, the conditions that increase vulnerability and the capacities available for protection. This distinction helps authorities decide where warning, evacuation assistance, shelters and other resources are most urgently needed.

A village may already know that a particular road floods during heavy rain. Risk assessment asks additional questions: Which households depend on that road? Is there another safe route? Are there people who cannot travel independently? Is suitable transport available? The answers convert general awareness into practical preparedness.

Participatory tools for gathering information

A participatory assessment involves residents in collecting and interpreting information about their locality. Common tools include:

  • Hazard mapping: identifying areas exposed to floods, coastal hazards, unsafe slopes or other locally relevant dangers.
  • Social mapping: locating settlements, public facilities and groups that may have different support needs.
  • Resource mapping: identifying usable shelters, safe water sources, transport, health facilities, communication facilities and trained volunteers.
  • Seasonal calendars: recording periods when particular hazards and livelihood difficulties are more likely.
  • Past-event histories: examining previous emergencies, including routes that became inaccessible and services that failed.
  • Community walks and consultations: checking conditions on the ground and obtaining information from residents who may not attend formal meetings.

These tools provide complementary information. A resource map does not replace a hazard map, and a list of households does not explain whether an evacuation route remains safe.

Identifying people who may need additional support

Disaster preparedness must recognise differential vulnerability: the same hazard can affect people differently because of mobility, health, income, age, social conditions, housing, language or access to services. It is more useful to identify the assistance required than to assume that every member of a broad category has identical needs.

People or situationPossible difficultyPreparedness arrangement
Persons with mobility disabilitiesInaccessible routes, vehicles or shelter entrancesAccessible evacuation arrangements and suitable shelter access
Older people living aloneDelayed receipt of warnings or lack of transportAgreed contact person, warning check and transport assistance
Pregnant women and people requiring treatmentInterruption of essential health servicesHealth-service contact, referral information and continuity planning
ChildrenSeparation from caregivers and difficulty understanding instructionsAge-appropriate information and family-reunification arrangements
Migrant workers and visitorsLimited knowledge of local routes or warning languageClear multilingual communication and accessible local information
Households in poorly protected housingGreater danger from the same hazardPriority assessment and appropriate safe-shelter arrangements

The presence of a disability, advanced age or pregnancy does not automatically determine a person's capacity or choices. People should be consulted about the support they require. Individuals may also possess important skills and be active contributors to preparedness.

Protecting personal information

Local authorities may need a confidential list of people requesting evacuation assistance. That list should be kept current, accessed only for legitimate preparedness and response purposes and shared only with people who need the information to provide assistance. Publicly displaying sensitive medical or household details is not necessary for effective risk mapping.

Turning assessment into decisions

Risk information should lead to specific arrangements: which households receive early contact, who checks the route, where transport is available, which shelter can accommodate different needs and who reports unresolved problems to local authorities. The assessment must be revised when people move, roads change or new risks appear.

If 2 settlements face the same expected flood level but only 1 has a usable evacuation road, they may require different transport and shelter arrangements. The hazard may be similar, but their capacities and practical risks differ.

Prelims focus

  • Hazard mapping identifies locations of danger; social mapping identifies people, settlements and facilities.
  • Resource mapping records available capacities such as shelters, transport and trained volunteers.
  • Seasonal calendars and past-event histories help identify when and how local hazards affect a community.
  • Differential vulnerability means that similar hazard exposure may produce different support needs.
  • Participatory assessment must include people whose concerns may be missed in general meetings.
  • Trap: Identifying a vulnerable group does not mean assuming that all its members are helpless or have identical needs.

[National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction, October 2024, Section 4.2.3, Participatory Risk Assessment, and Appendix II, Steps for Participatory Risk Assessment; National Council of Educational Research and Training, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 8, Local Governments, printed pp. 177–180. Official guidelines consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Participatory Risk Mapping and Identification of People Needing Assistance

body:
Why organised volunteers are important

People living near a disaster often begin helping before specialist response teams arrive. They may alert neighbours, guide residents towards a safe place, communicate urgent information and assist with relief arrangements. However, willingness alone does not make every activity safe. Effective volunteering requires defined roles, suitable training, coordination and attention to personal safety.

A community volunteer is a person who contributes time and effort to preparedness or response activities. Volunteers may work through a Village Disaster Management Committee, a local organisation, a recognised training programme or arrangements established by district authorities.

Typical community-level responsibilities

  • Awareness and warnings: sharing verified messages and checking whether intended recipients have understood them.
  • Assisted evacuation: helping people follow authorised routes and reach designated safe places.
  • Basic first aid: providing assistance appropriate to the volunteer's training and obtaining professional medical help when required.
  • Information collection: reporting blocked routes, urgent needs and missing services to the appropriate coordinator.
  • Relief support: helping organise supplies, communicate shelter arrangements and identify unmet needs.
  • Preparedness activities: maintaining contact lists, attending training and participating in drills.

Untrained residents should not undertake hazardous rescue operations merely because they are volunteers. Floodwater rescue, entry into damaged structures and other dangerous tasks require properly equipped and trained responders operating under appropriate authority.

Aapda Mitra and specialised response forces

Aapda Mitra is a Government of India programme for training community volunteers in disaster response and associated skills. It strengthens the availability of trained people at the local level and supports cooperation with district administration.

The Ministry of Home Affairs reports that the expanded Aapda Mitra scheme was sanctioned in March 2021 with an outlay of Rs 369.41 crore to train 100,000 volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts. Its scheme webpage reports that 100,000 volunteers have been trained. These are scheme-status figures reported on a webpage last updated on 28 October 2026, not permanent statutory numbers.

Aapda Mitra volunteers are distinct from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), which is a specialised disaster-response force. State disaster-response forces provide specialist capacity at state level under applicable arrangements. Trained community volunteers support response efforts; they do not become the NDRF merely by receiving volunteer training.

In Gujarat, the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority coordinates volunteer-development activities, including Aapda Mitra and Yuva Aapda Mitra programmes. Community volunteers can help connect official response arrangements with residents who need assistance.

Mock drills test preparedness before a real emergency

A mock drill is a planned exercise in which participants practise actions that would be required during an emergency. A drill is not the disaster itself. Its value lies in discovering practical problems while they can still be corrected.

For example, a school evacuation drill can test whether students recognise the signal, teachers know their responsibilities, exits are usable, assistance is available for students with disabilities and everyone can be accounted for at the assembly point. The arrangements should be explained in advance and suited to participants' ages and needs.

From preparation to improvement

Effective exercises have a clear objective and agreed responsibilities. Observers record delays, communication failures, inaccessible routes or confusion about where people should gather. A debrief, also called an after-action review, examines these observations and decides what to improve. The plan is then revised and, where useful, tested again.

Different exercises may test different capabilities. A communication drill checks whether warnings reach designated contacts. An evacuation drill examines movement and accountability. A shelter exercise may examine registration, access and basic facilities. Their purposes should not be confused.

Prelims focus

  • Volunteers support official disaster-management arrangements rather than replace specialised response forces.
  • Aapda Mitra is a community-volunteer training programme.
  • The expanded Aapda Mitra scheme was sanctioned in March 2021.
  • The Ministry of Home Affairs webpage updated on 28 October 2026 reports 100,000 trained volunteers in a programme covering 350 districts.
  • Mock drills test plans; debriefing identifies improvements for future exercises.
  • Trap: Conducting a drill does not establish that preparedness is adequate unless the findings are reviewed and acted upon.

[Ministry of Home Affairs, Aapda Mitra Scheme, scheme overview, webpage last updated 28 October 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction, October 2024, Sections 5.3 and 6, capacity development and stakeholder responsibilities; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Chapter XIII, Section 13.10, Aapda Mitra and Yuva Aapda Mitra Scheme. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
